newsitem.title: INDIA: India cyclone devastates crops in coastal state.
newsitem.headline: India cyclone devastates crops in coastal state.

text.p: Rice and other crops have been badly hit in a cyclone that lashed the southeastern Indian state of Andhra Pradesh but the full extent of damage was not immediately clear, officials said on Friday.
The cyclone hit the state's low-lying coastal areas on Wednesday night and raged for several hours before moving inland. Tropical storms are called cyclones in some parts of Asia and in Australia.
Authorities said the cyclone killed at least 510 people, destroyed tens of thousands of homes and devastated crops and livestock in an area mostly inhabited by many small farmers.
"The rice bowl of the state looks like a burial ground," the state's chief minister, V. Chandrababu Naidu, told reporters after an air survey of the worst hit areas on Thursday.
The United News of India news agency said the area, dotted with coconut and banana plantations and lush paddy fields, had been turned into a watery grave for "hundreds of people".
Around 3.5 million people live in the the fertile Konaseema region around the Godavari river delta, south of the port of Kakinada, which bore the full brunt of the storm.
A state agriculture ministry official told Reuters up to 400,000 hectares (988,000 acres) of standing rice paddy crops were hit by the cyclone.
Most of the crop was ready for harvesting and losses, because of swamping by sea water, could be long-term.

"The affected area of paddy will be about 300,000 to 400,000 hectares (741,000 acres to 988,000 acres) in the east and west Godavari districts, the state's main rice bowl," Vasudev Reddy, additional-director for natural calamities in Hyderabad, told Reuters in New Delhi.
"Coconut and banana are more seriously affected. The extent of damage is not known. We are still awaiting information." Reddy added.
About 500,000 hectares (1.25 million acres) are under paddy cultivation in the two districts. Nearly 2.6 million hectares (6.5 million acres) are under paddy in the whole state.
"How much area is fully affected and how much partially affected is still not known," Reddy said.
Rice is grown in nine districts of mainly low-lying Andhra Pradesh and the state contributes 15 percent of the country's total rice output, officials said.
S.M. Virmani, an agricultural expert at the Hyderabad-based International Crop Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Crops, said the sea water had moved inland to rice growing areas.
"Therefore, productivity losses on these lands will be definitely there for the next five years," he said.
Virmani said oilseed crops were not affected because harvesting of all the major oilseeds was over.

H.S. Brahma, the official coordinating relief operations from Hyderabad, said: "The entire Godavari district, especially the eastern district, will lose most of its paddy crop because of water-logging and high winds.
"For four hours, the wind speed during the cyclone was 130 to 145 kilometres per hour (81 to 91 mph), which hit standing crops," Brahma said.
Reddy Subramanium, a tax collector in Rajahmundry, east Godavari, said thousands of heads of livestock had been lost.
Apart from rice, he said 450,000 hectares of other crops, including chillies, banana plantations and coconut groves, had also been damaged.
Subramaniam said several thousand cattle were killed. "We have a problem on our hands with the dead animals -- whether to burn them or bury them," he said.
